strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: single-image full-head reconstruction under large viewpoint changes, while also exploring geometry/style-conditioned editing.

The reconstruction results are promising and consistent across several complementary metrics. On both Ava-256 and held-out NeRSemble identities, the method leads all reported baselines in PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace distance, with particularly large gains for extreme views. The qualitative comparisons broadly support improved robustness in occluded regions.

The hybrid use of real multi-view, synthetic multi-view, and diverse single-view training data is sensible. The ablation demonstrates that single-view-only training is inadequate and that the data sources provide complementary appearance and geometric supervision.

Using DINOv2 and SAM2.1 features as reconstruction supervision is practically useful. The ablation separates DINO-only, SAM-only, combined, and conventional LPIPS+L1 variants, showing complementary behavior and gains in DreamSim and identity preservation.

The shared lifting backbone, efficient Gaussian representation, and segmentation-map plus CLIP interface form a coherent system. The manuscript is generally clear, and limitations concerning animation, runtime, and baked lighting are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The editing contribution is not adequately validated. It is supported only by a small set of qualitative examples, with no comparison to editing baselines, quantitative measures of geometry preservation or style adherence, user study, or systematic tests of text prompts and reference images. Consequently, the claimed disentanglement is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The evaluation is small: only 11 Ava-256 and 5 NeRSemble identities are used, with no uncertainty estimates or per-subject results. The paper does not establish robustness across broader demographics, accessories, occlusions, lighting, image quality, or genuinely in-the-wild inputs.

All reconstruction metrics compare rendered images, despite strong claims about accurate and coherent 3D geometry. There is no direct geometry, depth, normal, or cross-view consistency evaluation. Because a learned 2D CNN refines each rendering, image-space improvements do not by themselves verify the stated geometric gains.

The ablation gives mixed evidence for the proposed loss. Without the CNN, LPIPS+L1 is better than the full loss in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, while the full loss is better in DreamSim and ArcFace. With the CNN, the full model still trails LPIPS+L1 in PSNR and SSIM. Thus the broad claim that foundation-model supervision is stronger than conventional losses depends on which metrics are prioritized.

Architectural originality is moderate: the system primarily combines established components, including DINO features, a MAE-style ViT, FLAME initialization, cross-attention lifting, Gaussian Splatting, PixelShuffle, and a rendering CNN. The most distinctive element is the DINOv2 plus SAM2.1 loss, whose advantage is useful but not uniformly established by the ablation.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a technical reconstruction paper. The manuscript omits loss equations and weights, optimizer and learning-rate settings, batch size, image resolution, decoder depth and width, attention details, dataset sizes and sampling ratios, camera handling, and model parameter count. The project-website field is blank, and no code or model-release statement is provided.

The paper claims temporal coherence from frame-wise application to two VFHQ sequences but reports no temporal metric or baseline. Likewise, runtime information is incomplete and the reported editing latency of 10–28 seconds weakens the characterization of the interface as interactive.

Overall, the reconstruction evidence is strong enough to show a worthwhile contribution, but the limited geometric validation, modest methodological novelty, and largely unsubstantiated editing/disentanglement claims leave the paper near the acceptance boundary rather than clearly above it.

strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult problem: efficient single-image full-head reconstruction that remains credible under large viewpoint changes, with an editing extension built on the same representation.

The reconstruction results are promising. On the reported extreme-view evaluation, the method substantially improves LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace distance over the strongest listed baselines on both Ava-256 and NeRSemble; the qualitative comparisons also show plausible completion of occluded regions.

The hybrid use of real multi-view, synthetic multi-view, and diverse single-view data is sensible, and the ablations at least attempt to separate the effects of training data, perceptual losses, and the CNN refinement stage.
The segmentation-plus-CLIP interface offers intuitive geometry and appearance control, and the demonstrated image- and text-conditioned outputs suggest potential practical usefulness.
weaknesses: The central claim that DINOv2/SAM supervision is stronger than conventional losses is not convincingly established. Without the CNN, the full loss is worse than LPIPS+L1 on PSNR (15.94 vs. 15.96), SSIM (0.7089 vs. 0.7228), and LPIPS (0.3010 vs. 0.2897), while its DreamSim advantage is only 0.0018; with the CNN, the pipeline again uses L1 and LPIPS supervision. Thus the experiments do not support the conclusion that conventional reconstruction or perceptual losses are unnecessary.

The editing contribution is evaluated only through selected qualitative examples. There is no comparison with editing baselines, user study, or quantitative measurement of text/image faithfulness, geometry preservation, factor disentanglement, identity retention, or multi-view consistency. The claim of strong disentanglement therefore remains largely asserted rather than demonstrated.

The reconstruction evaluation is too small to support broad state-of-the-art and generalization claims: it covers only 11 Ava-256 and 5 NeRSemble identities, reports no variability or statistical analysis, and uses NeRSemble both as a training source and as a held-out-identity benchmark. The criteria for selecting the five or sixteen evaluated views are insufficiently specified.

Evaluation fairness is difficult to verify. Methods have substantially different preprocessing and optimization regimes, the paper standardizes crops using PanoHead and changes GAGAvatar's background, but it does not clearly state how foreground masks, white backgrounds, image resolution, camera parameters, or failed tracking cases are handled for every method. These choices can materially affect all reported image-space metrics.

The ablation protocol is not controlled cleanly: the paper states that all ablations use a CNN trained on a previous model version, including the full model. This can bias comparisons, and no repeated runs are supplied to determine whether the small differences among several loss variants are meaningful.

Several important claims lack direct evidence. Geometry is assessed only through rendered-image metrics rather than surface, depth, landmark, or cross-view consistency measures; temporal consistency is claimed from two qualitative videos without a temporal metric; and the 2D refinement CNN makes it harder to attribute improved renders to better 3D geometry.

The method is underspecified for reproduction. Missing or unclear details include dataset sample counts and exact splits, construction of supervision for single-view FFHQ images, input/output resolutions, camera sampling, decoder depth and dimensions, attention details, optimizer and schedule, loss weights, feature layers/alignment, Gaussian initialization constraints, and inference time for reconstruction. The project-website field is also empty.

Originality is moderate: the system primarily combines established components—DINOv2/SAM features, a ViT cross-attention lifting decoder, FLAME initialization, Gaussian Splatting, CLIP conditioning, and a 2D refinement CNN. Such integration could still be valuable, but the limited and partly confounded validation does not presently demonstrate a sufficiently well-supported contribution for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: faithful single-image full-head reconstruction under large viewpoint changes, while also extending the representation to controllable 3D editing.

The reconstruction results are consistently strong. On both Ava-256 and NeRSemble, the method achieves the best reported PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace distance in both novel-view and extreme-view settings. The advantage is especially substantial for extreme views; for example, NeRSemble PSNR improves from 14.55 for the strongest baseline to 17.33, while ArcFace distance decreases from 0.3727 to 0.2588. The qualitative comparisons broadly corroborate these improvements.

Combining real multi-view data, synthetic multi-view data, and diverse single-view imagery is well motivated. The ablations clearly show that FFHQ-only training is insufficient for 3D consistency and that multi-view and single-view sources provide complementary benefits.

The architecture is technically coherent and practically appealing: a frozen general-purpose feature branch is complemented by a task-adaptive encoder, iterative cross-attention lifts image features to a canonical Gaussian representation, and foreground patch filtering reduces computation. Training on a single RTX 3090 also suggests reasonable accessibility.

The DINOv2-plus-SAM2.1 supervision is an interesting contribution. The component ablations show complementary behavior, and the full model attains the best ArcFace and DreamSim results among the loss variants. The editing demonstrations further indicate useful transfer of the learned 3D prior to reference- and text-conditioned generation.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective. The method diagram, viewpoint-stratified evaluation, explicit evaluation identities, and discussion of preprocessing make the central approach and empirical claims relatively easy to follow.
weaknesses: The evidence for editing and disentanglement is substantially weaker than that for reconstruction. It consists primarily of a small number of qualitative examples, with no comparison to editing baselines, quantitative preservation or controllability metrics, or user study. Moreover, a semantic segmentation map can encode appearance-related categories and CLIP features can encode shape, so the input design alone does not establish disentanglement.

The reconstruction evaluation is small: 11 Ava-256 identities and 5 held-out NeRSemble identities. Multiple views of the same identities are correlated, yet no per-identity results, error bars, or statistical tests are reported. This limits confidence in the generality of the claimed state-of-the-art performance, although the consistency and size of several reported gains remain persuasive.

Claims of accurate geometry and 3D consistency are evaluated only through rendered-image metrics. No direct geometric measure, cross-view correspondence test, depth or surface evaluation, or multiview consistency metric is provided. The view-conditioned 2D refinement CNN may also improve image metrics while introducing view-dependent behavior, which is not directly examined.

The central loss ablation is positive but not uniformly decisive. Without the CNN, LPIPS+L1 is better than the proposed loss in PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and slightly in DreamSim, while the proposed loss is clearly better mainly in ArcFace. With the CNN, the proposed method has better perceptual and identity metrics but worse PSNR and SSIM. In addition, every ablation uses a CNN trained on a previous full-model version, introducing a confound. Thus, the broad claim that foundation-feature supervision is generally stronger than conventional losses should be qualified.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details. The paper does not fully specify the DINOv2 and SAM loss aggregation and relative weights, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, batch size, sampling ratios and counts for the three training datasets, transformer dimensions and layer counts, CNN architecture, augmentation, or evaluation camera-selection protocol. Training times alone are insufficient to reconstruct the experiments.

Baseline breadth is somewhat limited for a 2026 submission, and several relevant cited systems are not evaluated. The paper also does not report parameter counts, reconstruction inference time, or memory usage. Reported editing latency is 10–28 seconds, but its hardware context is unclear; this weakens the practical efficiency discussion.

The frame-by-frame video consistency claim is supported only by two sequences and visual examples, without temporal metrics or a video baseline. It should be presented as a preliminary generalization observation rather than established temporal coherence. Likewise, baked lighting and the absence of relighting or dynamic expression control materially restrict avatar applications.

strengths: PercHead addresses an important and difficult problem: fast single-image full-head reconstruction that remains plausible under large viewpoint changes. The FLAME-anchored Gaussian representation, cross-attention decoder, mixed multi-view/in-the-wild training, and perceptual supervision form a coherent system.

The reconstruction evidence is fairly strong. On held-out Ava-256 subjects, the method leads all reported baselines in PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace for both novel and extreme views; similar gains appear on held-out NeRSemble identities. Improvements are especially large for extreme views, and extensive qualitative comparisons generally support the claimed robustness.

The ablations examine the principal design choices: 2D versus multi-view data, DINOv2 and SAM2.1 supervision individually and jointly, conventional LPIPS+L1 supervision, and the sharpening CNN. The conventional-loss model obtaining better LPIPS but worse DreamSim and ArcFace is informative evidence that the proposed supervision changes more than its optimized metric.

The editing extension is practically appealing: segmentation maps provide structural control while image or text embeddings control appearance. The qualitative grids demonstrate broad edits and reasonably consistent multi-view outputs, while the interactive interface improves potential usefulness.

The manuscript is visually clear and unusually transparent about several limitations, including baked-in illumination, lack of animation or temporal modeling, video flicker, and limited identity preservation during editing. Supplementary material provides training time, hardware, architecture dimensions, evaluated subject identifiers, cropping policy, and lightweight variants.
weaknesses: The evaluation population is small: quantitative results use only 11 Ava-256 subjects and five held-out NeRSemble identities, with no uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or subject-level statistics. Consequently, claims of statistically or broadly “significant” improvement are not established, even though the average margins are often convincing.

The editing contribution is supported almost entirely qualitatively. There is no quantitative evaluation of segmentation adherence, style or text alignment, identity preservation, geometry-style leakage, or user preference, and the NeRFFaceEditing comparison uses only one demo subject. The asserted disentanglement is particularly under-validated because geometry and style appear to come from the same image during training, making the factors correlated rather than explicitly disentangled.

The broad claim that the proposed loss is a drop-in replacement for conventional losses is not supported beyond this architecture and head-reconstruction domain. Within the reported ablation, its advantage over LPIPS+L1 is modest on DreamSim and ArcFace, worse on LPIPS, and demonstrated visually on only a few cases.

The loss definition in Eq. 7 multiplies the DINOv2 and SAM losses rather than adding them. A product permits optimization to suppress one factor and attenuates the other factor's gradient as either loss approaches zero. The paper neither motivates this unusual interaction nor compares it with a weighted sum, leaving an important technical choice insufficiently justified.

Image-space metrics and rendered-view examples do not directly verify recovered 3D geometry. No depth, surface, landmark, or multi-view geometric consistency metric is reported, so statements that the model “genuinely recovers” stable 3D structure are stronger than the evidence establishes, particularly because a learned sharpening renderer is applied after splatting.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful supplementary details: batch size, view-sampling protocol, image resolution, camera normalization and canonical coordinate handling, Gaussian attribute parameterizations, preprocessing thresholds, detailed sharpening-CNN architecture, and complete evaluation-view counts are not specified. These details are important for arbitrary-view reconstruction and fair baseline reproduction.

Some presentation errors create avoidable ambiguity: the editing-training sentence about feeding the same image “twice into CLIP and FFHQ” appears incorrect, Table 5 labels values around 15–16 as SSIM although they are evidently PSNR, and several percentage-change statements are difficult to parse. These are presentation refinements rather than rejection-level flaws.

strengths: The reconstruction results are promising: on Ava-256 and held-out NeRSemble identities, the method improves PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace over several relevant baselines, with particularly large gains for opposing or vertically shifted views. The qualitative comparisons likewise show fewer severe failures under large viewpoint changes.

The combination of FLAME-anchored Gaussians, cross-attention from a 3D-token decoder, mixed multiview/in-the-wild training, and a lightweight sharpening stage forms a coherent and practically useful system. Reported inference costs are reasonable, and lightweight variants are also examined.

The paper includes useful component ablations. In particular, it separately studies 2D versus multiview data, DINOv2 and SAM supervision, a conventional LPIPS+L1 objective, and the sharpening network. The loss analysis offers some evidence that DINOv2 and SAM features have complementary effects on hair, facial structure, and color artifacts.

The manuscript is generally understandable and provides several implementation details, including encoder and decoder dimensions, attention depth, optimization settings, training time, evaluation identities, and computational costs. Limitations concerning animation, temporal flicker, and baked-in illumination are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central loss is technically problematic as written. Equation 7 multiplies the DINOv2 and SAM losses rather than adding them. Minimizing a product does not require both terms to be small and can suppress the gradient of one term when the other becomes small, contradicting the claimed complementary supervision. If this is merely a typographical error, the actual training objective is still not reproducibly specified; if it is the implemented objective, its behavior requires analysis that is absent.

The main quantitative evidence is narrow: the supplementary material lists only nine Ava-256 subjects and five held-out NeRSemble identities, with no number of evaluated view pairs, variability, confidence intervals, or per-subject results. These very small samples make the broad state-of-the-art and robustness claims less convincing, especially because the paper emphasizes performance under diverse identities and extreme viewpoints.

The editing contribution is supported almost entirely by selected qualitative examples. There is no quantitative evaluation or user study of prompt adherence, geometry preservation, identity preservation, disentanglement, or multiview consistency. The only editing comparison uses one demo subject from NeRFFaceEditing, and the manuscript asserts that disentanglement 'emerges' without experimentally establishing it. This is a material evidentiary gap for one of the paper's two headline tasks.

The evaluation measures rendered 2D similarity but does not directly assess recovered geometry, cross-view consistency, or temporal stability. Consequently, statements that the method 'genuinely recovers a stable 3D representation' and maintains arbitrary-view consistency are stronger than the presented evidence. The video experiment consists of only two sequences and already exhibits acknowledged flicker.

The novelty is limited relative to the strength of the claims. Using frozen foundation-model activations as perceptual losses has prior precedent acknowledged by the paper, while the architectural backbone is closely based on existing ViT-to-Gaussian avatar models. Combining selected DINOv2 layers with SAM encodings is potentially useful, but the ablation shows modest metric gains over LPIPS+L1—while LPIPS+L1 is actually better on LPIPS and ties on PSNR—so claims that the proposed loss 'significantly' improves quality or challenges the need for conventional losses are overstated.

Important reproducibility and fairness details remain unspecified, including image resolution and batch size, dataset mixing and view-sampling ratios, exact SAM layers/tokens, the values of the Gaussian displacement bounds, the sharpening-CNN architecture, camera estimation/alignment procedures, and sufficiently detailed baseline configurations. Merely stating that code will be available does not resolve omissions in the submitted manuscript.

There are several clarity and consistency issues, including repeated text in the FaceLift discussion, numerous typographical errors, ambiguous notation, and an apparent inconsistency in Table 5 where the first metric is labeled SSIM despite values around 15–16 that appear to be PSNR. These are mostly presentation problems, but together with the loss-definition ambiguity they impede verification of the reported method.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult vision problem: high-fidelity, view-consistent 3D head reconstruction from one image, including challenging side-view inputs and large target-view changes.

The empirical reconstruction results are strong and consistent. On Ava-256, the method leads all reported baselines in PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace distance for both novel and extreme views; for example, extreme-view ArcFace improves from 0.416 for the strongest listed alternative to 0.282. Similar gains appear on held-out NeRSemble identities and against FaceLift.

The extensive qualitative results support the central view-consistency claim. Across frontal and side-view inputs, PercHead generally preserves identity, hair, facial geometry, and accessories more reliably than LGM, PanoHead, SphereHead, GAGAvatar, LAM, and FaceLift.

The proposed supervision based on intermediate DINOv2 and SAM 2.1 features is practically useful. The comparison with LPIPS+L1 shows improved DreamSim and ArcFace scores and visibly better high-frequency structure, while the individual DINOv2, SAM, token, data-source, and sharpening ablations help explain the respective contributions.

The architecture is technically coherent: FLAME-anchored Gaussian latents provide a useful geometric prior, cross-attention decouples image observations from the 3D representation, and the reconstruction model is efficiently adapted for segmentation- and CLIP-conditioned editing.

The supplement provides useful implementation and evaluation details, including architecture dimensions, training schedules, optimizer settings, evaluation identities, cropping and baseline-processing choices, runtime and memory measurements, and lightweight variants. Training on one RTX 3090 and the stated code release further strengthen practical reproducibility.

The editing interface is compelling and potentially useful: segmentation maps offer explicit structural control, while reference images or text provide appearance control. The presented grids demonstrate diverse, reasonably view-consistent results, including zero-shot text conditioning.
weaknesses: The reconstruction evaluation is based on only 11 listed Ava-256 identities and five held-out NeRSemble identities. Although multiple views may contribute samples, the manuscript does not state the exact number of evaluated image pairs or report variance, confidence intervals, or per-subject results. This limits confidence in the generality and statistical robustness of the reported margins.

The editing and claimed geometry/style disentanglement are supported almost entirely by selected qualitative examples. There is no quantitative evaluation of segmentation adherence, prompt or reference-image alignment, identity retention, leakage between geometry and style, or a user study. The single comparison with NeRFFaceEditing is also limited to one demonstration subject, making this part of the contribution less firmly established than reconstruction.

The perceptual loss is an incremental rather than fundamentally new construction: it combines cosine distances over frozen DINOv2 and SAM representations, and the paper acknowledges related DINO- and foundation-feature losses. Its value is demonstrated well in this application, but the broad claim that it is a drop-in replacement for conventional losses is not tested beyond this model and task.

Equation 7 defines the two loss terms multiplicatively rather than additively. This objective can weaken one signal when the other becomes small and is not theoretically or empirically justified against the conventional weighted sum. The authors should clarify whether this is the actual implementation and ablate product versus sum; this is a technical concern, not merely a typographical refinement.

Baseline fairness is not fully auditable. The paper explains cropping and GAGAvatar background processing, but does not specify all baseline versions, inference or inversion budgets, view-selection details, and whether hyperparameters were tuned comparably. This matters because several baselines were designed under different data and optimization regimes.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Qualitative examples cannot establish that unseen regions are accurately recovered rather than plausibly hallucinated, and frame-by-frame video consistency is asserted from two sequences despite acknowledged flicker and no temporal metric. Lighting remains baked into the representation, and expression transfer and temporal modeling are absent.

There are several correctable clarity issues: Table 5 labels a column as SSIM although values around 15–16 evidently correspond to PSNR; the main-paper percentage discussion around extreme-view ArcFace is difficult to parse; and exact preprocessing, dataset sampling, loss-backbone variants, and Gaussian attribute parameterizations should be consolidated for unambiguous reproduction.
